Thanks for the context  quick answers + recommended plan below. Long enough to be actionable, short enough for the Tue sync.

1) API return format
- Endpoint: POST /v1/rerank or /v1/ranking (we expose both verbs; payload includes candidate IDs + optional embeddings).
- Response: ordered list of items with: { id, score, normalized_score, metadata } and optional token_highlights when requested. Scores are model logits; normalized_score is a 0-1 sigmoid-scaled value for storage/analytics.

2) Candidate pool sizing & top_k
- Recommendation: generate ~100 candidates from retrieval (ANN/BM25 hybrid). Pass the full ~100 into the neural reranker, then render top_k to the user (start with top_k=5).
- Why: reranker cost scales linearly with candidates but quality gains saturate; 100 gives good recall while keeping latency manageable with batching & GPU optimization. If latency is tight, pre-filter to ~50.
- For A/B testing: try [baseline: BM25 top5] vs [BM25/ANN 100 -> rerank top5].

3) Embeddings vs reranker roles
- Use embeddings (dense retrieval) to find a high-recall candidate set. The neural reranker refines fine-grained ordering and supports contextual signals. Keep both: embeddings for recall, reranker for precision.

4) Evaluation metrics & thresholds
- Offline / offline eval: compute Precision@1, Precision@5, NDCG@5, NDCG@10, MRR. Also capture relative NDCG lift vs baseline.
- Thresholds to consider for safe rollout: P@1 improvement >= +0.05 absolute (or >= +10% relative) and NDCG@5 improvement >= +0.08 absolute. These are starting points  tune per query cohort.
- Track latency impact: measure 50/90/99 P50/P90/P99 for rerank call; aim for P90 <= 150ms for the rerank microservice.

5) Ranking APIs, tuning knobs, and observability
- We expose parameters: temperature/top_k for structured generation, rerank_top_k, return_scores=true/false, token_highlights=true/false, batch_size, and async mode for bulk offline scoring.
- We recommend versioned model pins for A/B and gradual rollouts; Redwood Console will show token-level cost and latency per-key.

6) Auth & SDK
- Auth: API Key is simplest for server-to-server; for multi-tenant setups we recommend per-tenant API keys stored in your KMS. OAuth2 is available for delegated access.
- SDKs: our JS/ Python SDKs support a .ranking method that accepts candidates + query + options. Sample flow:
  - Obtain API key
  - Initialize client with key (or service account)
  - Call client.rerank({ query, candidates, top_k: 5, return_scores: true })

7) Offline vs online testing
- Offline: use labeled holds (human judgments) or implicit feedback (CTR, click labels) to compute P@k and NDCG. Use stratified sampling by query type.
- Online: start with canary (5-10% traffic) and run an A/B test for 2 weeks or > 10k queries per cohort. Monitor business metrics + latency + error rates.

8) Quick implementation notes for ACME
- Start with a sandbox endpoint (we can provision today) and a default pipeline: BM25 + ANN -> pass 100 candidates -> rerank -> top 5.
- If you need highlights for UX, enable token_highlights on the rerank call; note it increases response size and some token-level compute.

Attaching a simple architecture diagram and the API reference PNG. Happy to drop a short JS and Python snippet into the HubSpot deal notes  will do that next.

Recommended thresholds summary: P@1 >= +0.05 absolute lift; NDCG@5 >= +0.08 absolute; P90 rerank <= 150ms.
